newsitem.title: USA: New Columbia/HCA CEO says to address investigation.
newsitem.headline: New Columbia/HCA CEO says to address investigation.

text.p: The new chairman and chief executive of Columbia/HCA Healthcare Co said Friday his main goals will be to address the government probe facing the company and focus on the interests of shareholders.

Dr. Thomas Frist also said he will bring a new style of management to the largest U.S. for-profit hospital company, as well as make an attempt to repair the company's relationship with government regulators.
"There is a trust level that is not there and we've got to quickly establish that with the authorities," Frist said in a press conference at company headquarters in Nashville, Tenn.

Columbia/HCA announced Friday morning that Frist had replaced long-time chairman and chief executive Richard Scott, who resigned Thursday, along with president and chief operating officer David Vandewater.

Of the resignations, Frist said, "In any institution, there is always time for a different style ... A series of events have occured. While there is no one precipitating factor, Mr. Rick Scott and Mr. David Vandewater, working with us, came to the conclusion that this was in the best interest of the company."
The Columbia/HCA board, of which Frist is a long-standing member, met into the late hours Thursday night to discuss concerns about Scott. Scott and Vandewater subsequently resigned.

Scott and Vandewater "had accomplished what they could," Frist said. "Maybe it might even have been an impediment, if they stayed, to the organization continuing to go forward, if they prolonged it any longer."

He said, "So together, that determination was made. Sure it's agonizing, but I applaud them. They had the courage to address it. It was time ... It was not a board action. It was them submitting their resignations."

Asked about the investigation that resulted last week in raids by federal agents to seize files at 33 company facilities in six states, Frist said, "My understanding and my belief is that Rick Scott and the people in this company have conducted themselves with the highest integrity. I have absolutely no knowledge of anything to the contrary."

Government agencies are looking into laboratory billing, home healthcare and other business practices at Columbia/HCA, which said earlier that five mid-level managerial employees in Florida have been subpoenaed to testify to a grand jury.
Frist added, "There are perceptions out there and there may be actual realities. I have to spend a great deal of time ... Let's find out what the facts are and let's correct them."
"All representations of those who have been with the company in leadership roles, they say they have no knowledge of any fraud or abuse," he said.
Columbia/HCA will have "zero tolerance" for any destruction of any company documents related to the investigation by government agents.

"We want to be cooperative. We want to do everything on our power to make information not only available to them, but on a timely basis. I can't stress that enough. I hope that's what's happened in the past, but I don't know," Frist said.

He declined to answer questions at the press conference about severance agreements for Scott and Vandewater, about any possible indictments of company officials in Florida and about reports that Columbia/HCA is in discussions with Tenet HealthCare Corp about a possible merger.

Contrasting himself with Scott and Vandewater, Frist said, "There is a clear difference in style...the way we go about things is different from the previous leadership. That doesn't mean their leadership was wrong. I'm just saying that, at this time, we're in a service industry, dealing with healthcare and peoples' lives and we need to have that perception out there that we do care."
